topic: Unlocking the Geometry of Networks: Planar Graphs and Euler’s Formula
target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Mathematics majors)

outline.topic: Unlocking the Geometry of Networks: Planar Graphs and Euler’s Formula
outline.target_audience: University students (Computer Science or Mathematics majors)

sections.title: Introduction: The Map-Maker's Challenge
sections.content: Define a Planar Graph (a graph that can be drawn without edges crossing). Connect this to real-world applications like printed circuit board design or subway map layouts.
sections.example: Visualize a simple subway map of 3 stations where tracks cross—show how rearranging nodes makes it planar.

sections.title: Core Components: Vertices, Edges, and Faces
sections.content: Introduce the anatomy of a planar graph. Define 'Faces' as the enclosed regions, including the infinite 'outer face'. Emphasize that these components are the building blocks of the formula.
sections.example: A triangle (3 vertices, 3 edges) has 2 faces: the inner triangle and the infinite area surrounding it.

sections.title: Euler’s Characteristic Formula
sections.content: Present the fundamental theorem: V - E + F = 2. Explain that this elegant constant holds true for all connected planar graphs regardless of their complexity.
sections.example: Use an animation of a square with a diagonal: V=4, E=5, F=3. Calculation: 4 - 5 + 3 = 2.

sections.title: The Concept of Dual Graphs
sections.content: Explain how to construct a Dual Graph: create a new vertex inside every face of the original graph and connect them across shared edges. Connect this to symmetry and topological transformations.
sections.example: An animation showing a hexagon honeycomb grid transforming into a set of connected triangles (the dual).

sections.title: Summary & Application
sections.content: Review the relationship: Properties of the original graph (V, E, F) directly dictate the properties of the dual graph (V', E', F'). Conclude with the importance of these tools in graph coloring and network reliability.
sections.example: Show a circuit diagram being simplified using duality to check for signal interference paths.
